Fit an ordinary least-squares model bundle

Source: R/lm-fit.R
fit_linear.Rd

Fits stats::lm() to one dataset, or once per imputation of stacked long-form data, and combines imputations with Rubin's rules. A single fit is inferred on the t distribution with its residual degrees of freedom, as PROC REG reports it. Pooled coefficients use Barnard and Rubin's degrees of freedom, described below.

Usage

fit_linear(
  formula,
  data,
  outcome_col = NULL,
  id_col = "id",
  imputation_col = NULL,
  prediction_col = "fitted"
)

Arguments

formula

Model formula. The response may be transformed, e.g. log(los) ~ age. A . on the right-hand side expands to the data's other columns, excluding the response, id_col and imputation_col.

data

A data frame, or stacked imputations when imputation_col is set.

outcome_col

Outcome column. By default the one variable in the formula's response; if supplied, it must name that variable. The response must read exactly one column.

id_col

Patient identifier column. Required only when imputation_col is set.

imputation_col

Imputation-index column, or NULL for one dataset.

prediction_col

Name of the fitted-value column added to $data, averaged across imputations.

Value

An object of class c("rm_fit", "ps_data"). $tables$fit_quality gives each fit's residual degrees of freedom, residual standard error and R-squared; R-squared is NA for imputed data, where Rubin's rules define none.

Pooled degrees of freedom

With imputation_col set, each pooled coefficient is tested against a t distribution, and the df column of $tables$estimates gives its degrees of freedom. We use Barnard and Rubin's (1999) small-sample degrees of freedom, computed the way mice::pool() computes them, so a pooled table here and one from mice agree.

Rubin's (1987) original degrees of freedom are \(\nu_{old} = (m - 1) / \lambda^2\), where \(m\) is the number of imputations and \(\lambda = (1 + 1/m) B / T\) is the proportion of a coefficient's total variance \(T\) due to missing data, through the between-imputation variance \(B\). (This is lambda in mice, not its finite-sample fraction of missing information, fmi.) When little is missing, \(\lambda\) is small and \(\nu_{old}\) can run into the millions, larger than the sample could ever support, and the intervals come out too narrow. Barnard and Rubin cap it with the complete-data degrees of freedom \(\nu_{com}\), the value the analysis would have had with no missing data: $$\nu_{obs} = \frac{\nu_{com} + 1}{\nu_{com} + 3} \nu_{com} (1 - \lambda), \qquad \nu = \left(\frac{1}{\nu_{old}} + \frac{1}{\nu_{obs}}\right)^{-1}.$$ So \(\nu\) never exceeds \(\nu_{com}\), and it approaches \(\nu_{old}\) as \(\nu_{com}\) grows.

\(\nu_{com}\) is \(n - k\), the residual degrees of freedom of the first imputation's model: \(n\) analysed patients minus \(k\) estimated parameters. That holds for every family, linear, logistic, ordinal, nominal and count, as it does in mice. nnet::multinom() reports no residual degrees of freedom, so for a nominal model \(k\) is its effective degrees of freedom, again as mice does. Pooling stops with an error when \(\nu_{com}\) is zero or negative, as it is for a saturated model, because no small-sample degrees of freedom exist then.

Two consequences are worth knowing. First, a single logistic, ordinal, nominal or count fit is tested against the normal distribution (df is Inf), but the same model pooled over imputations reports a finite df and a t test. A single linear fit uses its residual degrees of freedom. Second, SAS PROC MIANALYZE reports \(\nu_{old}\) unless you give it the complete-data degrees of freedom with EDF=. To reproduce these df, and the p-values and intervals that depend on them, run PROC MIANALYZE with EDF= set to \(n - k\).

Barnard J, Rubin DB (1999). Small-sample degrees of freedom with multiple imputation. Biometrika, 86(4), 948–955. doi:10.1093/biomet/86.4.948

Rubin DB (1987). Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys. Wiley. doi:10.1002/9780470316696

See also

fit_logistic(), bs_continuous()

Examples

dta <- sample_ps_data(n = 150, seed = 42)
fit <- fit_linear(ef ~ age + female, data = dta)
fit$tables$estimates[, c("term", "estimate", "std.error", "p.value")]
#>          term   estimate  std.error      p.value
#> 1 (Intercept) 68.7280984 5.12425021 2.156296e-32
#> 2         age -0.1867446 0.06779147 6.237331e-03
#> 3      female  0.1259720 1.20495525 9.168075e-01
